score: 70 recommendations: 63 judged and agreeing with the original on the dataset, 7 not judged, 0 observed wrong; 1 estimated cheaper, and it ran 1.30x faster
metric: KumoSQL's recommended rewrites (the rule pipeline and the proof-gated optimizer) on 103 TPC-DS and 53 DSB statements, judged in a fixed order: correctness first (proof label, then same rows when executed against the original), then the EXPLAIN cost estimate, then measured runtime, each reported on its own.
correctness: No wrong result observed under the recorded comparison policy, on one workload (PostgreSQL scale factor 1, seed 7): 63 of 70 recommendations were judged by the row comparator and agreed with the original (same rows; ordered queries compared on their sort keys, ties in any order, when the keys are output columns); 7 rule rewrites were not judged because the original no longer runs on PostgreSQL after the BigQuery round trip the rules need. Proof and dataset agreement are separate facts: 66 of the 70 carry a proof; 4 are unproven (CTE inlining around window functions), of which 3 ran and returned the same rows and 1 (q21) was not judged. Agreement on one dataset is evidence, not a proof, and a proof holds only under its stated assumptions
usefulness: Rules: 44 recommendations (27 parenthesis removals, 24 single-use CTE inlinings), all estimated unchanged and none 10% faster or slower; they simplify text, not plans. Optimizer: 26 recommendations, 1 estimated cheaper (DSB multi_block query069, -11%) and it ran 1.30x faster; of the 25 estimated unchanged, none ran faster and 1 ran 0.90x (TPC-DS q58, 1.06x in the first run, so timing noise)
performance: Median of 5 alternating runs after a warm-up on PostgreSQL 16, TPC-DS and DSB at scale factor 1; geometric-mean speedup 1.006x (rules, 37 judged) and 0.997x (optimizer, 26). The estimate predicted the one real saving and no false ones
caveats: What "0 wrong" covers: 44 rule and 26 optimizer recommendations on 103 TPC-DS and 53 DSB statements; it excludes build recommendations, shared-model proposals, cost attribution and change reports. The proof holds under its model (declared keys and NOT NULL hold, floats are never NaN, runtime errors are not modeled, rows tied under ORDER BY or LIMIT may be chosen differently), and the optimizer accepts a rewrite whose estimate is up to 2% higher, so accepted does not mean cheaper. These assumptions are copied into every record the tool writes now. The saved numbers come from the first comparator, which accepted four pairs it should not have (none seen in the 70): ORDER BY ASC against DESC on a key that is not projected, output columns renamed, floats differing by less than 5e-10, and a looser predicate that agrees on the data (WHERE k = 10 against k < 15). The comparator now appends hidden sort keys and compares output column names and types, so the first two are rejected (regression tests in tests/test_cost_validity_bench.py); floats still compare rounded to 9 decimal places and agreement on one dataset can never rule out the last. That comparator has not been run on this workload: the TPC-DS and DSB data, queries and PostgreSQL are not available in the environment that made the change, so the score and date are those of the first run and 0 wrong is not yet confirmed under the stricter comparison. Estimates are PostgreSQL EXPLAIN costs, a local stand-in for BigQuery dry-run bytes; no real BigQuery run yet. Queries generated with DSB's dsqgen (seed 7) and not stored in the repo (TPC licence). One optimizer rewrite (TPC-DS q44) first compared as different rows because tied rows came back in another order; it returned identical rows on re-run, and the comparison now allows ties in any order.
